---
title: "The Three Credentials"
subtitle: "Which password opens what, and how to recover each one"
---

AppBay has three passwords. They are deliberately independent, they are never synchronized
with each other, and each is recovered by a different command.

Mixing them up is the most common way to lock yourself out of something while holding a
password that works perfectly well for something else.

## The two domains

| | What it opens | Where it lives | Recover with |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Edge user** | The apps you deployed — **and the AppBay UI** | the edge's identity store | `appbay edge users reset-password` |
| **Master password** | `vault.enc`, your encrypted secrets | `var/lib/secrets/master-password` | `appbay secrets vault rotate-password` |

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A[operator] -->|signs in to AppBay| E[Edge user]
  U[your users] -->|sign in to deployed apps| E
  A -->|unlocks secrets| V[Master password]

  E --> EF[edge identity store]
  V --> VF[vault.enc]
```

::: {.callout-note}
## There used to be three

A separate **control-plane account** opened the AppBay UI, stored in
`etc/control-plane/users.yaml` and reset with `appbay admin reset-password`. RFC-001 §1 removed
it: the UI is a stack behind the edge like Portainer or Open WebUI, so it authenticates the same
way they do. One store, one place to revoke someone.

Its edge route carries an **admin-only** policy (`authp/admin`), narrower than an app's default,
because the control plane is the one stack that can reach the container runtime socket. So
"can open Grafana" still does not mean "can reconfigure the installation" — that distinction
moved from a separate password to a role.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Why the remaining two stay separate
Signing in is not the same as decrypting. Someone who can reach the UI should not thereby hold
the key to every secret in the vault, and the vault must stay openable by the CLI on a host
where no edge is running at all. AppBay never syncs them.
:::

## Which one do I want?

**"I can't log in to the AppBay UI."**

That is an edge user, same as any app. RFC-001 §1 removed AppBay's separate control-plane
account: the web UI sits behind the Caddy Security edge like Portainer or Open WebUI, so
there is no second password and no `etc/control-plane/users.yaml`.

```bash
appbay edge users reset-password alice --generate --reveal
```

⚠️ Only members of `authp/admin` can reach the control plane — its edge route carries an
admin-only policy, narrower than an app's default, because it is the one stack that can reach
the container runtime socket.

If the UI says it is *not reachable through the edge*, that is a deployment problem rather than
a login one: the server refuses to serve when nothing has authenticated the request. Run
`appbay init --ingress-provider caddy`, set `domain:` in `etc/system.yaml`, then
`appbay server start`.

**"An app asks me to sign in and my password doesn't work."**

That is an edge user — a person who signs in to a *deployed app*, not to AppBay.

```bash
appbay edge users list
appbay edge users reset-password alice --generate --reveal
```

**"A deploy failed saying a secret could not be resolved."**

That is the vault password.

```bash
appbay secrets vault rotate-password
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## A lost vault password is unrecoverable
`vault.enc` is encrypted with it. Rotation *re-encrypts* using the current password, so it
requires the current one. There is no reset — losing it means losing the stored values,
though the references to them in your manifests remain intact.
:::

## Reading a password prompt correctly

Every command that takes a password accepts three forms, and the difference matters:

```bash
# From a pipe — the value never appears in argv
printf %s "$SECRET" | appbay edge users reset-password alice --password-stdin

# Generated and shown exactly once
appbay edge users reset-password alice --generate --reveal

# Generated and NOT shown (for automation that will set it elsewhere)
appbay edge users reset-password alice --generate
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why `--password-stdin` exists
Passing a secret as a command argument puts it in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, where every local
user can read it for the life of the process. Fine for a throwaway value in your own shell;
not fine for a configuration-management run seeding real credentials on a shared host.
:::

## What survives what

| Event | Edge users (incl. UI access) | Vault |
|---|---|---|
| Delete `appbay.db` (the cache) | unaffected | unaffected |
| Rotate the master password | unaffected | re-encrypted |
| Switch edge provider | store is edge-specific — see migration | unaffected |
| Reinstall AppBay, same `$APPBAY_HOME` | survives | survives |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Deleting the cache is safe
`appbay.db` holds job history and a query mirror — all disposable. Since RFC-001 §1 it holds no
credentials and no sessions at all: identity comes from the edge on every request, so deleting
the database does not even log anyone out.
:::

## Retired commands

`appbay authelia`, `appbay auth` and `appbay admin` are gone. Running any of them prints what
replaced it and exits non-zero, so a script that still calls them fails rather than appearing to
succeed.
